title: Receiver front end: on-die resistive termination plus differential input buffer
topology: An on-die termination (ODT) resistor pair, matched to the incoming transmission line's characteristic impedance, sits directly at the receive pads (either as a fixed resistor or, more commonly, a digitally-trimmed parallel resistor bank to correct for process/temperature variation) to absorb the incoming signal and suppress reflections; the termination node feeds directly into a differential input buffer -- typically a resistively- or actively-loaded differential pair biased for wide common-mode input range -- that presents high input impedance beyond the termination point, amplifies the (often small, channel-attenuated) incoming swing, and squares it up to full-swing CMOS/CML levels for the downstream clock-data-recovery and data-sampling circuitry.
spec_class: PHY-class receive front end -- input termination and buffering stage for high-speed serial/wireline I/O (serdes, LVDS-class, chip-to-chip links) that sets the receiver's input impedance match, common-mode range, and first-stage noise/sensitivity budget

pdk_portability.notes: The termination-resistor-plus-differential-buffer topology is fully portable; any PDK with precision or trimmable resistors and matched core devices can implement it, and sky130 provides both. The digitally-trimmed termination-resistor bank's step size and range must be re-derived from sky130's specific resistor-option process variation (poly/diffusion resistor tolerance), and the input buffer's common-mode input range and offset are set by sky130's specific device Vt/mismatch characteristics, so both need re-simulation against sky130 models; the trim-calibration architecture itself (a small resistor DAC plus a comparator-based calibration loop) is PDK-independent.

sizing_approach: Set the nominal termination resistor value to match the line's characteristic impedance (e.g. 50 ohm single-ended / 100 ohm differential), then add a small trim resistor bank (binary- or thermometer-weighted parallel legs) sized to correct the nominal resistor's process-corner spread back to within the impedance-match tolerance the link budget requires (typically a few percent); size the input differential pair's devices for sufficient transconductance to resolve the smallest expected input swing after channel attenuation, while keeping input capacitance low enough that it does not itself become a significant reflection source at the termination node; bias the input buffer's common-mode operating point to sit centered in its available input range across the expected DC common-mode variation from the driver/channel (e.g. AC-coupled links still need a self-biased common-mode restoration point), and budget input-referred offset/noise against the minimum eye opening the downstream sampler needs to resolve.
layout_idioms: termination resistors placed as close to the receive bond pad / bump as physically possible, since any trace length between the true termination point and the pad reintroduces the reflection the termination is meant to suppress
differential input buffer laid out symmetrically on a common axis with the termination resistors and pads, matching routing length/parasitics on both legs to preserve common-mode rejection
guard ring around the sensitive input buffer's differential pair, isolating it from substrate noise injected by adjacent digital (CDR, deserializer) circuitry that shares the same PHY macro

trim-resistor-bank switches placed adjacent to their resistor legs with short routing to the shared termination node, so switch parasitic capacitance does not itself distort the intended termination impedance at high frequency

source.citation: C.-K. K. Yang, R. Farjad-Rad, and M. A. Horowitz, "A 0.5-um CMOS 4.0-Gbit/s serial link transceiver with data recovery using oversampling," IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 33, no. 5, pp. 713-722, May 1998.
source.license_or_openness: Peer-reviewed IEEE journal paper cited here for its receiver front-end termination and input-buffering approach only (no figures or text reproduced), per the KB's open-sources sourcing rule. This is a widely-cited early CMOS serial-link transceiver paper whose receive front end (on-chip termination feeding a differential input buffer ahead of oversampled data recovery) established the front-end architecture that later serdes receiver designs continue to build on.

notes: This entry covers only the analog front end (termination plus buffering); it hands off a full-swing differential signal to whatever clock-data-recovery/sampler architecture the rest of the PHY uses, which is out of scope here. See cml-tx-line-driver for the transmit-side counterpart whose matched output impedance this entry's termination is designed to receive into -- together they form a matched-impedance point-to-point link's two ends.
